label: <DEL> step of maximum-length (L=9) sequences
explanation: Fires almost only on the delimiter step (input <DEL>), and 98% of activations / 99.4% of mass come at L=9 (t=9), where it fires on about 76% of sequences. A small weak tail fires at the <DEL> step of L=8 sequences (t=8, 0.6% of mass, low activation). Essentially never active during the original or copy phases (1 stray activation), and never at <DEL> for L<=7. Which tokens were seen changes the rate only weakly: firing becomes a bit more likely as the number of digits in the sequence grows (0.8x lift with 0 digits up to about 1.9x with 4+), and the first or output token barely matters (lift about 1.2-1.3x). This reads as a detector for a long sequence ending, i.e. the delimiter after 9 inputs.

issues: The explanation's claims match the data. On the dev split, 12888 of 12889 activations fall on the <DEL> step: 99.4% of activation mass is at t=9 (L=9), 0.6% is a weak tail at the <DEL> step of L=8 sequences (which fires on about 1.4% of those sequences), and there is 1 stray activation in the original phase. There are none in the copy phase and none for L<=7. On the test split the predicate scores precision 0.764, recall 0.980, F1 0.859.

The test-split misses are all the L=8 <DEL> tail, worth 0.7% of the mass. The 3918 false positives are L=9 <DEL> steps with no visible shared pattern; it reads as graded, partial firing rather than a missing class of cases.

The first-token modulation is a bit stronger than 'barely matter' suggests. Restricting to L=9 <DEL> with first_tok in {w,a,z,k,b,c} raises precision to 0.91, but recall falls to 0.24. That is a lift of about 1.2x within the L=9 <DEL> steps, which still matches the stated 1.2-1.3x, so this is a minor point, not a refutation.

The digit modulation checks out. Adding n_digits>=1 gives F1 0.72 (precision 0.75), and the digit-free subset has precision 0.79, so splitting on digits does not sharpen the predicate. No better predicate was found.
